newsitem.title: ITALY: Confident Prodi launches Italian euro committee.
newsitem.headline: Confident Prodi launches Italian euro committee.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi launched a new Treasury committee on Friday to pave the way for the single European currency and brushed aside doubts in German banking circles about Italy's chances of making the grade.
Prodi told the strategic committee's inaugural session that it had to guarantee Italian institutions were fully primed for the planned launch of the euro currency in 1999.

"The European Union is making an unprecedented commitment and no country can allow itself to fall behind, leaving others to clear the way," he told the meeting in an elegant Treasury chamber which was opened to reporters and EU ambassadors.
"For too long Italy has been unable to make contributions which bear any relation to its size...but the government now intends to remedy this," he added.

Senior German bankers have openly questioned whether debt-ladden Italy should be let into the first wave of countries lining up for European economic and monetary union (EMU), with some suggesting its membership be delayed until 2002.
But Prodi, who flew to Bonn on Thursday for a brief meeting with German chancellor Helmut Kohl, said politicians would ultimately decide which countries were in the EMU "A' team.

"These big decisions are not made by central banks but by governments," Prodi said, adding that Kohl had assured him he wanted Italy to make "rapid, effective" progress towards joining the single currency from day one.
As a step towards getting the country in shape for the euro, Prodi promised that the lira would return to the European exhange rate mechanism (ERM) by the end of the year.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said the re-entry rate would reflect the lira's level against other leading currencies in the preceding weeks and months.

Italian businessmen, worried that recent lira gains have made their exports uncompetitive, are pushing for as weak a central parity rate as possible, while the French, looking to boost their own industry, want the lira to appreciate further.
A Reuter poll of analysts this week showed that the market was expecting a parity of around 1,000 lire per German mark, slightly weaker than the present 995 lire level.
The lira was pushed out of the ERM in a 1992 currency crisis and the exact timing of its return is likely to depend on how the government's 1997 austerity budget fares in parliament.

The package, which is designed to hack 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit, has to be ratified by parliament before the end of the year. But ministers expect much of the voting to be completed by the end of November.
Ciampi said the belt-tightening budget confirmed Italy's determination to put the economy on an even footing.

He said that only countries with a "culture of stability" would be able to enter the elite euro club, adding that this culture depended on control of public spending, central bank autonomy and an incomes policy.

"Today, Italy can say that it has practically established all three," Ciampi said, adding that he fully supported a proposed stability pact to keep countries' economies in line once they became part of the euro zone.

However he said EU partners should not just follow rigid financial guidelines before unleashing potentially painful fines on errant states. "Personally, I believe that rigid numerical criteria would be dangerous," he said. "(The pact) must be qualitative, and not quantitative." $1 = 1,535 lire
